new_note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:6). *And the disciples were astonished at his words. But Yahusha (Jesus) answereth again, and saith unto them, Children, how hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of Elohim (God)!* (Mark 10:24). Sirach does not say gold is evil; he says it has ruined many, and that their destruction was standing right beside them while they held it. Yahusha (Jesus) puts his finger on the same spot: not the riches, but the trusting in them. The hand that closes around gold is the hand that cannot take hold of the kingdom, and the disciples were astonished because the whole world around them measured blessing by that very gold.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:6 — *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present..* The ruin is in the trusting; *how hard is it for them that trust in riches* (Mark 10:24).

new_note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:6). *No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Luke 16:13). Sirach had already watched gold ruin many before Yahusha (Jesus) said no servant can serve two masters. The ruin Sirach names is what happens to the man who takes mammon for a master; it does not share him, it destroys him, and the destruction is already present while he thinks he is being served. The steward in the parable just before this verse was called wise because he treated money as a thing that perishes and used it, instead of bowing to it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:6 — *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present..* The servant of mammon in Luke 16:13 walks into the ruin Sirach names.

new_note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:7). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach speaks of men who sacrifice to gold. He names it as a thing worshipped, an altar men bring offerings to, and he says it trips every fool who goes near it. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can set mammon across from Elohim (God) as a rival master: mammon in that sentence is not a neutral tool but a master that takes those who serve it, the very stumblingblock Sirach saw men sacrificing to. You cannot keep an altar to both.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:7 — *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it.* Gold as a master men sacrifice to; *Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon* (Matthew 6:24).

new_note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:7). *It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of Elohim (God).* (Mark 10:25). Sirach says gold is a stumblingblock to those who sacrifice to it, and every fool is taken by it, taken as a bird is taken in a snare. Yahusha (Jesus) says the rich man passes into the kingdom about as easily as a camel through a needle's eye. The two sayings are one picture: a man held by what he sacrifices to cannot get through the narrow door, because the thing holding him will not fit. It is not the gold that stops at the needle's eye; it is the man who will not let go of it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:7 — *every fool shall be taken with it.* The one taken by his gold cannot pass the needle's eye of Mark 10:25.

new_note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:7). *No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Luke 16:13). Sirach calls gold a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it. He is describing worship, an offering brought and a devotion given, and he says that devotion takes its devotee. Yahusha (Jesus) names the same thing when he calls mammon a master. To serve mammon is to sacrifice to the stumblingblock; the servant does not own it, it owns him, and Sirach had already said where that ends.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:7 — *them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* To serve mammon (Luke 16:13) is to sacrifice to the stumblingblock.

new_note: *Blessed is the rich that is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:8). *Then Yahusha (Jesus) beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.* (Mark 10:21). Sirach calls the rich man blessed who is found without blemish and has not gone after gold, and the next verse asks, who is he? as if such a man were rare enough to go looking for. Yahusha (Jesus) looked at a rich young man, loved him, and put Sirach's question to him in the flesh: sell what you have, give to the poor, and come. The man went away grieved, because his great possessions had him. The blessing Sirach names was offered to him on the road and he could not take it, because he had gone after gold and the gold had gone after him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:8 — *Blessed is the rich that is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold..* The rich young ruler of Mark 10:21 was offered that blessing and went away grieved.

new_note: *If you sit at a bountiful table, be not greedy upon it, and say not, There is much meat on it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:12). *And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite.* (Proverbs 23:2). Solomon tells the man given to appetite to put a knife to his own throat when he sits at a ruler's table; Sirach tells him not to be greedy at a bountiful table or to say, There is much meat here. It is the same instruction in two voices, generations apart. A full table is a test of the eye and the hand, and both wisdom writers lay the restraint on the guest, not on the host.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:12 — *If you sit at a bountiful table, be not greedy upon it.* Solomon's knife to the throat (Proverbs 23:2) is the same restraint at the same table.

new_note: *If you be made the master of a feast, lift not thyself up, but be among them as one of the rest; take diligent care for them, and so sit down.* (Ecclesiasticus 32:1). *And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,* (Matthew 23:6). Sirach's rule for the master of a feast is to be among the guests as one of the rest and to take diligent care for them before he sits down. Yahusha (Jesus) names the scribes and Pharisees by the opposite habit: they love the uppermost rooms at feasts and the chief seats in the synagogues. Sirach put the care of the company first and the seat last; the leaders of that day had put the seat first and the company nowhere. The one who washed his disciples' feet on the night he was betrayed was keeping Sirach's rule to the letter.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 32:1 — *lift not thyself up, but be among them as one of the rest.* The uppermost rooms at feasts (Matthew 23:6) are the opposite of Sirach's master of the feast.

new_note: *As the clay is in the potter’s hand, to fashion it at his pleasure: so man is in the hand of him that made him, to render to them as liketh him best.* (Ecclesiasticus 33:13). *Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?* (Matthew 20:15). Sirach says man is in the hand of his Maker as clay is in the hand of the potter, to render to each as seems best to him, and the verse before it says he has blessed and exalted some and brought others low. The householder in the parable asks the grumbling labourers the same thing: is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? The one who made the clay owes it no explanation for how he shapes it. An eye that goes evil because the Maker has been good to another has forgotten whose hand it is in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 33:13 — *As the clay is in the potter’s hand, to fashion it at his pleasure.* The householder's right over his own (Matthew 20:15) is the potter's right over the clay.

new_note: *Set him to work, as is fit for him: if he be not obedient, put on more heavy fetters.* (Ecclesiasticus 33:28). *Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury.* (Matthew 25:27). Sirach's counsel for a servant is to set him to work fit for him, and if he will not obey, to bind him tighter; idleness, the verse before says, teaches much evil. The master in the parable judges his servant by the same measure. The servant was not condemned for losing the money; he was condemned for doing nothing with it, when even handing it to the exchangers would have been work enough. The one who was given a charge and buried it is the one Sirach's heavier fetters were written for.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 33:28 — *Set him to work, as is fit for him: if he be not obedient, put on more heavy fetters..* The servant of Matthew 25:27 was judged for doing nothing with his charge.

new_note: *He that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten, his offering is ridiculous; and the gifts of unjust men are not accepted.* (Ecclesiasticus 34:18). *But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.* (Matthew 12:7). Sirach says the offering of a thing wrongfully gotten is laughable before Yahuah (God), and the gifts of unjust men are not received. Yahusha (Jesus) told the Pharisees that if they had understood I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, they would not have condemned his hungry disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath. Both lines say the same thing about the altar: it does not wash the hands that bring to it. A sacrifice offered while mercy is withheld from the guiltless is the unjust man's gift, and Yahuah (God) does not take it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 34:18 — *the gifts of unjust men are not accepted.* Sacrifice while condemning the guiltless (Matthew 12:7) is the gift Yahuah (God) does not take.

new_note: *Whoso brings an offering of the goods of the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father’s eyes.* (Ecclesiasticus 34:20). *He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor.* (Proverbs 28:8). Sirach says the man who brings an offering out of the goods of the poor is like one who kills a son in front of his father. Solomon says the man who grows rich by usury and unjust gain is only gathering it up for someone who will pity the poor. Both are talking about the same money. Taken from the poor and carried to the altar it is an abomination; held by the one who took it, it will not stay, for by the hand of Yahuah (God) it ends up with the merciful, and the one who gathered it is left with nothing but the blood on his hands.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 34:20 — *Whoso brings an offering of the goods of the poor.* Unjust gain only gathers for the merciful (Proverbs 28:8); offered at the altar it is bloodshed.

new_note: *So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and goes again, and doeth the same: who will hear his prayer? or what does his humbling profit him?* (Ecclesiasticus 34:26). *And Yahusha (Jesus) said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.* (Matthew 9:15). Sirach asks what a man's fast profits him when he fasts for his sins and then goes back and does the same; who will hear his prayer? When John's disciples asked why his disciples did not fast, Yahusha (Jesus) did not do away with fasting; he said the days would come when they would fast. But he placed it after the bridegroom is taken, in the grief of a people who have truly lost something, not as a routine kept while nothing changes. Sirach had already named the difference: a fast that turns from the sin is heard, and a fast that returns to it is noise.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 34:26 — *a man that fasteth for his sins, and goes again, and doeth the same: who will hear his prayer?.* Fasting that turns is heard; *then shall they fast* (Matthew 9:15) is fasting with the loss truly felt.

new_note: *He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough: he that takes heed to the commandment offers a peace offering.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:1). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says the man who keeps the law has already brought offerings enough, and the one who takes heed to the commandment has offered a peace offering. That is the key to what Yahusha (Jesus) meant by I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, which he took from Hosea. He was not setting mercy against the Torah; mercy is the Torah kept, and the Pharisees who kept the altar while despising the publicans and sinners at his table had kept the smaller part and dropped the greater. The commandment kept is the offering Yahuah (God) wanted all along.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:1 — *He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough.* Mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:13) is the commandment kept, which is the offering.

new_note: *He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough: he that takes heed to the commandment offers a peace offering.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:1). *But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.* (Matthew 12:7). Sirach says keeping the law is bringing offerings enough, and heeding the commandment is itself a peace offering. Yahusha (Jesus) quotes Hosea, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, against men who condemned the guiltless for picking grain on the Sabbath. Nothing in either verse loosens the Sabbath or the altar. What both say is that the man who holds the form of the commandment while condemning the hungry has not kept the commandment at all, and his sacrifice counts for nothing, while the one who shows mercy has brought the offering.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:1 — *he that takes heed to the commandment offers a peace offering.* Heeding the commandment is the offering; mercy over sacrifice at Matthew 12:7.

new_note: *He that requiteth a goodturn offers fine flour; and he that gives alms sacrificeth praise.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:2). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says that to repay a good turn is to offer fine flour and to give alms is to sacrifice praise. These are the altar's own words, fine flour and the sacrifice of praise, set on ordinary acts of kindness. When Yahusha (Jesus) told the Pharisees to go and learn what I will have mercy, and not sacrifice means, Sirach had already written out the lesson. Mercy shown is sacrifice offered, and the man who gives alms has stood at the altar whether he knows it or not.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:2 — *he that gives alms sacrificeth praise.* Alms as sacrifice; *I will have mercy, and not sacrifice* (Matthew 9:13).

new_note: *To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to Yahuah (God); and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:3). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Sirach says departing from wickedness pleases Yahuah (God) and forsaking unrighteousness is a propitiation; the turning itself is the atonement. Yahusha (Jesus) says he came to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous, in the same breath as I will have mercy, and not sacrifice. The publicans at his table who turned had made the offering Sirach describes; the men standing outside objecting to the company had brought their sacrifices and left the turning undone.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:3 — *to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.* The turning is the offering; Matthew 9:13 calls sinners to that repentance.

new_note: *The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:6). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the offering of the righteous makes the altar fat and its sweet savour rises before the Most High. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father who sees in secret, and he rewards them openly. The altar is the same in both: it is the Most High who receives, and he receives what is righteous, not what is displayed. An offering made for men to see never reaches that altar; the one made where only he looks is the sweet savour.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:6 — *the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* Alms in secret (Matthew 6:4) reach the same Most High who receives the righteous offering.

new_note: *The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:7). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the sacrifice of a just man is accepted and its memorial is never forgotten. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father, who repays openly. The reward of being seen by men is spent the moment it is received; the memorial Sirach speaks of is kept by the Most High, who does not forget. The just man's offering goes into a record that outlasts him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:7 — *the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* The Father who sees in secret (Matthew 6:4) keeps the memorial men never saw.
flag: Live text misprint: Ecclesiasticus 35:7 reads 'acceptable. and the memorial' (period for comma); quoted as it stands.

new_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:8). *The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.* (Matthew 6:22). Sirach tells the worshipper to give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye and not to cut short the firstfruits of his hands. The good eye is an old Hebrew way of speaking of generosity, the eye that is not grudging and does not measure what it gives. Yahusha (Jesus) speaks of the single eye that fills the whole body with light, and the verses around it are about treasure and about mammon. A good eye in giving and a single eye in the body are the same eye; it looks at Yahuah (God) and his honour, and the hand follows where it looks.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:8 — *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye.* The good eye in giving is the single eye of Matthew 6:22.

new_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:8). *Honour Yahuah (LORD) with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:* (Proverbs 3:9). Sirach is repeating Solomon almost word for word. Honour Yahuah (LORD) with what you have and with your firstfruits, Solomon says; give Yahuah (God) his honour and do not diminish the firstfruits of your hands, says Sirach, and he adds the good eye, the ungrudging eye, as the manner of it. The first and the best belong to Yahuah (God), and they are not to be cut short. The proverb came down whole, and Sirach handed it on whole.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:8 — *diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* Proverbs 3:9's firstfruits, kept whole and given with a good eye.

new_note: *Do not think to corrupt with gifts; for such he will not receive: and trust not to unrighteous sacrifices; for Yahuah (God) is judge, and with him is no respect of persons.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:12). *And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.* (Matthew 21:13). Sirach says do not think to corrupt Yahuah (God) with gifts, for he will not take them, and do not trust in unrighteous sacrifices, for he is judge and shows no favour to persons. Yahusha (Jesus) walked into the temple courts and found the house of prayer turned into a den of thieves; the gifts and the sacrifices had become a trade. The leaders who ran that trade trusted that the sacrifices would still cover them. Sirach had already told them the judge does not take bribes, and the King overturning the tables was the judge saying it in person.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:12 — *Do not think to corrupt with gifts; for such he will not receive.* The den of thieves (Matthew 21:13) was gifts and sacrifices turned to trade, and the judge will not take them.

new_note: *He will not despise the supplication of the fatherless; nor the widow, when she poureth out her complaint. Do not the tears run down the widow’s cheeks? and is not her cry against him that causeth them to fall?* (Ecclesiasticus 35:14–15). *A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.* (Matthew 12:20). Sirach says Yahuah (God) does not despise the fatherless when they plead or the widow when she pours out her complaint. Matthew is quoting Isaiah about the servant who will not break a bruised reed or put out a smoking wick, and he says it of Yahusha (Jesus) in the same chapter where the Pharisees are plotting to destroy him. The ones who cause the tears and the one who hears them stand side by side. The widow's cry Sirach speaks of is heard by the same one who would not break a reed already bent.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:14 — *He will not despise the supplication of the fatherless; nor the widow.* The bruised reed not broken (Matthew 12:20) is the same mercy toward the ones who cry.
flag: Moved from 35:13 to 35:14: the old note quoted the fatherless-and-widow verse, which in the live text is 35:14, not 35:13 ('He will not accept any person against a poor man'). The old note's second sentence (the tears on the widow's cheek) is not in live 35:14 either; only 35:14 is quoted. Cold read: the widow's-tears line is live 35:15 — quoted 35:14–15 as a range (card sits at 35:14).

new_note: *Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:19). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach says Yahuah (God) will not rest until he has rendered to every man according to his deeds and judged the cause of his people and made them rejoice in his mercy. Yahusha (Jesus) says the Son of Adam will come in the glory of his Father and reward every man according to his works. The two halves Sirach holds together are the two halves the King names: a reckoning by works for every man, and vindication and joy for his own people. Reward comes at his coming and it comes by deeds, and those who are his rejoice in mercy on that day rather than in a reckoning they skipped.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:19 — *Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds.* Reward according to works at the Son of Adam's coming (Matthew 16:27).

new_note: *Have mercy upon us, O Yahuah (God) of all, and behold us:* (Ecclesiasticus 36:1). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). Sirach opens his great prayer with a cry for mercy to the Elohim (God) of all, and the prayer goes on to ask that all the tribes of Jacob be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says he was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel). The one being asked for mercy in Sirach's prayer is the one who answered it in person, sent to the very scattered house the prayer was about. Behold us, Sirach prays; the Shepherd came looking for the sheep.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:1 — *Have mercy upon us, O Yahuah (God) of all, and behold us.* The prayer for mercy that the mission to the lost sheep (Matthew 15:24) answers.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 8:11). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and given back their inheritance as from the beginning, twelve tribes and not two. Yahusha (Jesus) says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. The many from east and west are the children of those three fathers coming home from where they were scattered, which is exactly what Sirach asked for. They are not a new people put in the seat of Yashar'el (Israel); they are the tribes of Jacob taking their own seats at their fathers' table.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning..* The many from east and west (Matthew 8:11) are the tribes coming home to their fathers' table.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). Sirach prays for the gathering of all the tribes of Jacob, back into the inheritance as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says he was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel). The prayer and the mission have the same object: not Yahudah (Judah) alone, who had a temple and a land, but the whole house that had been scattered and lost among the nations. The prophets promised it, Sirach prayed it, and the King came for it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *inherit you them, as from the beginning.* The lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) in Matthew 15:24 are the tribes Sirach prayed home.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And Yahusha (Jesus) said unto them, Verily I say unto you, That ye which have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Adam shall sit in the throne of his glory, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 19:28). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the twelve that in the regeneration, when the Son of Adam sits on the throne of his glory, they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Yashar'el (Israel). Twelve thrones for twelve tribes means the twelve tribes are there to be judged: gathered, whole, as from the beginning. What Sirach asked for in prayer the King states as the shape of the kingdom when it comes.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together.* Twelve thrones for twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28); the tribes gathered whole.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of Elohim (God) shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.* (Matthew 21:43). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the chief priests the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth its fruits; a nation, one, not the nations. That one nation is the gathered tribes of Jacob bearing fruit, the very people Sirach prayed for. It is not the church put in the place of Yashar'el (Israel), and it is not whoever keeps Torah regardless of seed; it is Jacob's own tribes, gathered home and bearing the fruit their leaders in that day would not bring.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *inherit you them, as from the beginning.* The one nation bringing forth fruit (Matthew 21:43) is the gathered tribes of Jacob, not a replacement.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.* (Mark 13:27). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and given back their inheritance as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says the Son of Adam will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the earth to the other. The four winds are where the tribes were scattered; the elect gathered out of them are the tribes Sirach prayed home. The prayer names who; the gospel names how and when.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together.* The elect gathered from the four winds (Mark 13:27) is this prayer answered.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *He hath holpen his servant Yashar'el (Israel), in remembrance of his mercy;* (Luke 1:54). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Mary, carrying the child, sings that he has helped his servant Yashar'el (Israel) in remembrance of his mercy. The help she sings is the beginning of the answer to Sirach's prayer: mercy remembered toward the whole servant Yashar'el (Israel), all the tribes, not a figure of speech for some other people. The gathering was being set in motion in her womb.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *inherit you them, as from the beginning.* Mary's *he hath holpen his servant Yashar'el (Israel)* (Luke 1:54) is this prayer beginning to be answered.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of Elohim (God).* (Luke 13:29). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says they will come from east, west, north and south and sit down in the kingdom of Elohim (God). Four directions is where the tribes went; four directions is where they come back from. The ones sitting down are the tribes Sirach prayed for, the firstborn his next verse names, not a substitute people set at their table.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together.* From east, west, north and south (Luke 13:29) the scattered tribes sit down at home.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *For the Son of Adam is come to seek and to save that which was lost.* (Luke 19:10). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. Yahusha (Jesus) says the Son of Adam came to seek and to save that which was lost. What was lost was the house, the tribes scattered until they forgot who they were, and seeking them is the gathering Sirach prayed for. He said it in the house of Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham his neighbours had written off, which is what a found tribe looks like one man at a time.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *inherit you them, as from the beginning.* To seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10) is to gather the tribes Sirach prayed for.

new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad.* (John 11:52). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and inherited as from the beginning. John says Yahusha (Jesus) would die not for that nation only but to gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad. The scattered children are Jacob's tribes among the nations; the one nation in the land was Yahudah (Judah). Sirach prayed for the gathering, and John names the death that pays for it; Caiaphas said more than he knew.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together.* The children of Elohim (God) scattered abroad (John 11:52) are the tribes this prayer asks home.

new_note: *O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:12). *And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 8:11). Sirach prays for mercy on the people called by the name of Yahuah (God), on Yashar'el (Israel) whom he named his firstborn. Yahusha (Jesus) says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. The firstborn is one people, named from the beginning, and the many from east and west are that firstborn's scattered children coming to their fathers' table. The mercy Sirach asks for the firstborn is the seat Yahusha (Jesus) says they will take.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:12 — *Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* The firstborn's scattered children sit down with the fathers in Matthew 8:11.

new_note: *O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:12). *He hath holpen his servant Yashar'el (Israel), in remembrance of his mercy;* (Luke 1:54). Sirach asks mercy for the people called by the name of Yahuah (God), for Yashar'el (Israel) his firstborn. Mary sings that he has helped his servant Yashar'el (Israel) in remembrance of his mercy. The mercy prayed for and the mercy remembered fall on the same people, the firstborn son, the servant, and both are tied to the gathering: Sirach's verse before asks for all the tribes of Jacob, and Mary's next lines name the oath sworn to Abraham. The firstborn is remembered, not replaced.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:12 — *have mercy upon the people that is called by your name.* Mercy remembered toward his servant Yashar'el (Israel) in Luke 1:54.

new_note: *O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:12). *For the Son of Adam is come to seek and to save that which was lost.* (Luke 19:10). Sirach asks mercy for Yashar'el (Israel), the firstborn called by the name of Yahuah (God). Yahusha (Jesus) says the Son of Adam came to seek and to save that which was lost. The firstborn had been scattered until he was lost, Hosea's not my people, and the mercy Sirach prayed for arrived as a Shepherd out looking for him. The one sought is the firstborn; the seeking is the mercy.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:12 — *whom you have named your firstborn.* The lost whom the Son of Adam seeks (Luke 19:10) is the firstborn scattered.

new_note: *Fill Sion with your unspeakable oracles, and your people with your glory:* (Ecclesiasticus 36:14). *And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the Son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of Yahuah (Lord); Hosanna in the highest.* (Matthew 21:9). Sirach prays for Sion to be filled with the oracles of Yahuah (God) and his people with his glory, in the same prayer that asks for the tribes to be gathered and for mercy on Jerusalem. When Yahusha (Jesus) rode into the city the multitudes cried Hosanna to the Son of David and Blessed is he that cometh in the name of Yahuah (Lord), and the next verse says all the city was moved. The glory Sirach asked to fill Sion came through its gate on a colt. The city was moved and did not know by whom; the prayer was being answered in its streets.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:14 — *Fill Sion with your unspeakable oracles, and your people with your glory.* The glory entered the city at Matthew 21:9 to the cry of Hosanna.

new_note: *Is it not a grief to death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy?* (Ecclesiasticus 37:2). *And Yahusha (Jesus) said unto him, Friend, wherefore art thou come? Then came they, and laid hands on Yahusha (Jesus), and took him.* (Matthew 26:50). Sirach asks whether it is not a grief unto death when a companion and friend turns enemy. In the garden Yahusha (Jesus) called Judas Friend as the kiss was given and the hands were laid on him. He had just said his soul was exceeding sorrowful, even unto death, which is Sirach's own measure of it. The friend who had eaten his bread lifted up his heel against him, and the King named him Friend to the last; that is the grief Sirach meant.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 37:2 — *when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy.* *Friend, wherefore art thou come?* (Matthew 26:50) is this grief spoken in the garden.

new_note: *My son, in your sickness be not negligent: but pray to Yahuah (God), and he will make you whole.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:9). *And, behold, a woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment:* (Matthew 9:20). Sirach tells the sick man not to be negligent but to pray to Yahuah (God), who will make him whole. The woman with the issue of blood had been sick twelve years, and she came behind Yahusha (Jesus) and touched the hem of his garment, and he turned and told her that her faith had made her whole. She was not going around Sirach's counsel; she was doing it. The one who spoke and walked with the fathers was standing in the crowd in flesh, and reaching for his garment was her prayer to Yahuah (God).
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 38:9 — *pray to Yahuah (God), and he will make you whole.* The woman who touched the hem (Matthew 9:20) made that prayer with her hand.
flag: Theology correction: the old note called the woman's touch an 'inversion' or 'bypass' of Sirach's pray-first counsel. Rewritten: Yahusha (Jesus) is the Formed one who spoke in the Tanakh, so reaching for him is the prayer Sirach prescribes, not a way around it.
